video.title: One phone, many pupils: Pairs, roles and live coding
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — computer studies teacher, Kenya (main character)
Ms Amina Bello — primary teacher, Nigeria (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: Forty-five pupils and eight phones, borrowed from parents for the afternoon. If one pupil holds each phone, thirty-seven of them sit and watch. So every pupil gets a job.
Today: pair programming, group roles and live coding, for classes with few devices.

In pair programming, two pupils share one device. The driver types or taps. The navigator reads, checks every line and thinks about what comes next. They swap roles every five to ten minutes, so both do both.

With four pupils to a phone, add two more roles. The tester tries inputs that might break the program. The reporter writes down what worked and what didn’t, and shares it with the class. Rotate the roles each task.

Pairs aren’t just a way to share devices. Studies in universities found that pairs produced better programs and more students stayed with programming. Talking about code out loud catches bugs early. And many beginners say they feel more confident.

With one phone, code live from the front. Hold the phone up or copy the code onto the board as you type. Stop before each run and ask: what will happen? Make a mistake on purpose, and let the class find it.
Quick check! A pair has worked for twenty minutes, and the same pupil has typed the whole time. What should happen?
Swap! Set a timer, or swap at each task. Both pupils must do both jobs. And watch that the navigator really navigates: reading, checking, suggesting, not just watching.

Prepare phones the day before, where there’s a connection. Download the lessons you’ll use, and open one code step once, so Python is saved for offline use. In class, everything then runs with no internet.
Debugging is a great job for pairs. The navigator reads the error message aloud. The driver points to the line. Together they agree on one change before running again.

scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: bug hunt, in pairs
scenes.narration: In the app, open Bug hunt and play it in pairs. The navigator reads each error aloud; the driver fixes it. Swap after every bug, and talk about bug three, the one with no error message.
Your turn. Tomorrow’s class has no internet. What must you do today?

Download today. Remember: in pairs, a driver and a navigator swap every few minutes. In fours, add a tester and a reporter. Code live from the front, and let the class predict. And prepare phones the day before.

Try it in class tomorrow: one programming task in pairs or fours, with role cards. Set a timer to swap roles every seven minutes. At the end, ask each reporter for one thing that worked and one bug they found.

checkpoints.prompt: A pair has worked 20 minutes; the same pupil typed all along. What should happen?

options.text: Nothing: the faster typist should type
They should swap every 5 to 10 minutes
The navigator should get their own phone

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — swapping often means both pupils do both jobs and learn both.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — without swaps one pupil does all the typing and the other drifts. Swap every 5 to 10 minutes.

checkpoints.prompt: Tomorrow’s class has no internet. What must you do today?

options.text: Download the lessons and open a code step once

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — downloaded lessons and one Python run while online let everything work offline.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — lessons and Python need one download while online; after that they work offline.
